strengths: PST addresses a meaningful gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender-role associations in images containing two people. Extending the analysis from occupations to organizational hierarchy adds a useful perspective.

The occupational audit covers 800 ordered prompts across 40 occupations and counterbalances left/right placement. The reported increase in stereotype adherence from SS 10.00 to 47.38 provides substantive descriptive evidence of a difference between generation settings.

Three human annotators assess each image, with reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92. Checking BLIP against human judgments and declining to rely on its poor paired-image performance strengthens the evaluation.

The appendices provide descriptor inventories, prompt templates, annotation instructions, and disaggregated results, making the proposed procedure understandable. Source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b01/review-experiment-rtujwz6d/call-dff5e08609484ac784d87d9d51ef19db/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The interpretation of SS overstates what it measures. SS is signed stereotype adherence, rather than an absolute measure of departure from gender balance. Opposing imbalances cancel: Table 2 averages female SS 50 and male SS −30 into an apparently low overall score of 10. Consequently, low single-subject SS does not establish fairness. Likewise, calling individual stereotype-consistent images 'biased' conflates an instance with a distributional property; even independent, gender-balanced generation would produce at least one stereotype-consistent person in 75% of pairs.

The single-subject baseline uses only three images per identity, making occupation-level comparisons and selected illustrative examples highly uncertain. Table 10 reports run results but no confidence intervals or inferential analysis. The large aggregate occupational difference is suggestive, but smaller organizational-power differences and detailed amplification claims need repeated, matched sampling and uncertainty estimates that account for paired observations.

The annotation protocol measures perceived gender at requested positions without reporting independent verification that the intended occupations and hierarchical roles were actually depicted there. Role swaps, extra people, or ambiguous role realization could affect the conclusions. Although annotators can select 'Cannot Identify,' its frequency, treatment in score denominators, and label aggregation procedure are unspecified.

Some quantitative reporting needs reconciliation. Under the stated definitions, Figure 4’s occupational percentages imply SS = 71.9 + 74.3 − 100 = 46.2, whereas Table 2 reports 47.38. Different exclusions or denominators might explain this, but none are documented. Section 3.2.2 also states 944 prompts despite describing 800 occupational and 1,152 organizational-power prompts.

Reproduction of the reported results is insufficiently specified for a changing proprietary service. The manuscript omits the generation interface and date, handling of any prompt rewriting, and precise organizational-role samples and matching across conditions. The promised code and data release would help, but the current description leaves consequential implementation choices unresolved.

The mitigation conclusions exceed the experiment: one intervention is tested, with occupational evaluation restricted to the five most biased occupations per gender. An organizational-power SS of −11.12, without uncertainty estimates, does not establish reliable reverse bias or a general failure of prompt-based mitigation. The useful DALLE-3 case study leaves a close Findings case, but the measurement interpretation and evaluation gaps prevent a clear positive recommendation.
